sections.title: Emotional overload: Added complexity
sections.context: You are speaking with someone who is very distressed. They talk quickly, repeat themselves, and jump between points. They sound tearful and occasionally raise their voice. You have limited time and you need to understand what they actually need, but you also want them to feel supported and not shut down. There is some time pressure, and one detail may need to be checked before you move on.

rows.label: Best response
rows.response: Calmly acknowledge how they feel, slow the pace, and ask one clear question at a time to regain structure. Keep the response calm, structured, and focused on the next confirmed detail.

rows.label: Worst response
rows.response: Interrupt firmly and tell them to calm down so you can understand them. This deals with the immediate pressure by ending, redirecting, or taking firm control of the exchange.

sections.title: Incomplete information: Added complexity
sections.context: Someone asks you for help but gives vague or inconsistent details. When you ask clarifying questions, they become frustrated and say, “I’ve already explained this.” You suspect you’re missing something important and you need accuracy, but you don’t want to escalate their frustration. The person sounds frustrated, but you still need enough detail to act accurately.

rows.label: Best response
rows.response: Explain why clarity matters and ask focused follow-up questions to confirm the key details. Keep the response calm, structured, and focused on the next confirmed detail.

rows.label: Worst response
rows.response: Stop asking questions and make assumptions so you can move forward. This deals with the immediate pressure by ending, redirecting, or taking firm control of the exchange.

sections.title: Pressure to bypass process: Added complexity
sections.context: A person is stressed and insists you should bypass a standard process “just this once.” They say it’s urgent and they don’t have time for the normal steps. You understand their pressure, but you also know the process exists for a reason. A quick response may help, although missing a key fact could cause problems later.

rows.label: Best response
rows.response: Explain calmly why the process exists and follow it while still offering support and urgency. Keep the response calm, structured, and focused on the next confirmed detail.

rows.label: Worst response
rows.response: Delay the process without explaining why. This moves things forward quickly by working from the details already available.

sections.title: Identifying a potential issue: Added complexity
sections.context: During a non emergency call, something doesn’t quite add up. The caller hasn’t said anything directly concerning, but a detail conflicts with what they said earlier. You’re not sure whether it’s a misunderstanding or something important. Others nearby appear busy and you have to decide how to handle it. You need to balance reassurance with keeping control of the conversation.

rows.label: Best response
rows.response: Ask a clarifying question to check your understanding and resolve the inconsistency. Keep the response calm, structured, and focused on the next confirmed detail.

rows.label: Worst response
rows.response: Ignore it — it’s probably nothing. This deals with the immediate pressure by ending, redirecting, or taking firm control of the exchange.

sections.title: Hostile communication: Added complexity
sections.context: A caller becomes angry and starts blaming you personally for not helping fast enough. They raise their voice and interrupt you. You can feel tension rising, but you still need to progress the conversation and keep it productive. There is some time pressure, and one detail may need to be checked before you move on.

rows.label: Best response
rows.response: Acknowledge their frustration, stay calm, and refocus the conversation on what happens next. Keep the response calm, structured, and focused on the next confirmed detail.

rows.label: Worst response
rows.response: Match their tone to assert control. This deals with the immediate pressure by ending, redirecting, or taking firm control of the exchange.

sections.title: Compassion vs boundaries: Added complexity
sections.context: A victim shares something very personal and emotional. They ask you to promise that a specific outcome will happen because they need reassurance. You want to support them, but you can’t guarantee outcomes. The person sounds frustrated, but you still need enough detail to act accurately.

rows.label: Best response
rows.response: Show empathy, explain you can’t make promises, and focus on what you can do right now. Keep the response calm, structured, and focused on the next confirmed detail.

rows.label: Worst response
rows.response: Promise the outcome to reassure them. This deals with the immediate pressure by ending, redirecting, or taking firm control of the exchange.

sections.title: Decision-making under uncertainty: Added complexity
sections.context: You need to decide on next steps but you don’t have all the information. Waiting could reduce risk, but delaying could also make things worse. You must balance action with accuracy and responsibility. A quick response may help, although missing a key fact could cause problems later.

rows.label: Best response
rows.response: Take a proportionate step while continuing to gather information. Keep the response calm, structured, and focused on the next confirmed detail.

rows.label: Worst response
rows.response: Act immediately using the information available. This moves things forward quickly by working from the details already available.

sections.title: Correcting a mistake: Added complexity
sections.context: Partway through a conversation with a caller, you realise you misunderstood something earlier. You notice the misunderstanding could affect what you do next. You feel slightly embarrassed, and the caller is still talking. You need to balance reassurance with keeping control of the conversation.

rows.label: Best response
rows.response: Correct yourself calmly and clarify the accurate information. Keep the response calm, structured, and focused on the next confirmed detail.

rows.label: Worst response
rows.response: Ignore it to avoid drawing attention to the mistake. This deals with the immediate pressure by ending, redirecting, or taking firm control of the exchange.

sections.title: Competing priorities: Added complexity
sections.context: On an emergency call, you’re dealing with one urgent situation when another equally urgent issue demands your attention at the same time. You feel pulled in two directions and need to prevent anything being dropped. There is some time pressure, and one detail may need to be checked before you move on.

rows.label: Best response
rows.response: Manage both by setting expectations and prioritising based on risk, communicating clearly. Keep the response calm, structured, and focused on the next confirmed detail.

rows.label: Worst response
rows.response: Avoid deciding and hope someone else takes responsibility for the second situation. This deals with the immediate pressure by ending, redirecting, or taking firm control of the exchange.

sections.title: Emotional self-control: Added complexity

sections.title: Ambiguous responsibility: Added complexity

sections.title: Information overload: Added complexity
sections.context: A caller provides a large amount of information very quickly. Some details are clearly important, others may be irrelevant. You’re concerned you’ll miss key points if you don’t structure the conversation. A quick response may help, although missing a key fact could cause problems later.

sections.title: Personal frustration: Added complexity

sections.title: Uncertainty about next steps: Added complexity

sections.title: Emotional overload: Added complexity
sections.context: You are speaking with someone who is very distressed. They talk quickly, repeat themselves, and jump between points. They sound tearful and occasionally raise their voice. You have limited time and you need to understand what they actually need, but you also want them to feel supported and not shut down. There is some time pressure, and one detail may need to be checked before you move on.

rows.label: Best response
rows.response: Let them continue uninterrupted so they feel heard, even if it takes time. This helps with one part of the exchange and keeps momentum, but it may not confirm every key point.

rows.label: Worst response
rows.response: End the conversation quickly and refer them elsewhere. This moves things forward quickly by working from the details already available.

sections.title: Incomplete information: Added complexity
sections.context: Someone asks you for help but gives vague or inconsistent details. When you ask clarifying questions, they become frustrated and say, “I’ve already explained this.” You suspect you’re missing something important and you need accuracy, but you don’t want to escalate their frustration. The person sounds frustrated, but you still need enough detail to act accurately.

rows.label: Best response
rows.response: Explain why clarity matters and ask focused follow-up questions to confirm the key details. Keep the response calm, structured, and focused on the next confirmed detail.

rows.label: Worst response
rows.response: Accept the information as given to avoid upsetting them further. This moves things forward quickly by working from the details already available.

sections.title: Pressure to bypass process: Added complexity
sections.context: A person is stressed and insists you should bypass a standard process “just this once.” They say it’s urgent and they don’t have time for the normal steps. You understand their pressure, but you also know the process exists for a reason. A quick response may help, although missing a key fact could cause problems later.

rows.label: Best response
rows.response: Delay the process without explaining why. This moves things forward quickly by working from the details already available.

rows.label: Worst response
rows.response: Agree to bypass the process to help them quickly. This deals with the immediate pressure by ending, redirecting, or taking firm control of the exchange.

sections.title: Identifying a potential issue: Added complexity
sections.context: During a non emergency call, something doesn’t quite add up. The caller hasn’t said anything directly concerning, but a detail conflicts with what they said earlier. You’re not sure whether it’s a misunderstanding or something important. Others nearby appear busy and you have to decide how to handle it. You need to balance reassurance with keeping control of the conversation.

rows.label: Best response
rows.response: Assume the worst and escalate immediately. This helps with one part of the exchange and keeps momentum, but it may not confirm every key point.

rows.label: Worst response
rows.response: Ignore it — it’s probably nothing. This deals with the immediate pressure by ending, redirecting, or taking firm control of the exchange.

sections.title: Hostile communication: Added complexity
sections.context: A caller becomes angry and starts blaming you personally for not helping fast enough. They raise their voice and interrupt you. You can feel tension rising, but you still need to progress the conversation and keep it productive. There is some time pressure, and one detail may need to be checked before you move on.

rows.label: Best response
rows.response: Match their tone to assert control. This deals with the immediate pressure by ending, redirecting, or taking firm control of the exchange.

rows.label: Worst response
rows.response: End the interaction because they are being disrespectful. This moves things forward quickly by working from the details already available.

sections.title: Compassion vs boundaries: Added complexity
sections.context: A victim shares something very personal and emotional. They ask you to promise that a specific outcome will happen because they need reassurance. You want to support them, but you can’t guarantee outcomes. The person sounds frustrated, but you still need enough detail to act accurately.

rows.label: Best response
rows.response: Change the subject to avoid making things more emotional. This moves things forward quickly by working from the details already available.

rows.label: Worst response
rows.response: Avoid responding directly to their request and move on. This helps with one part of the exchange and keeps momentum, but it may not confirm every key point.

sections.title: Decision-making under uncertainty: Added complexity
sections.context: You need to decide on next steps but you don’t have all the information. Waiting could reduce risk, but delaying could also make things worse. You must balance action with accuracy and responsibility. A quick response may help, although missing a key fact could cause problems later.

rows.label: Best response
rows.response: Wait until you have complete certainty before doing anything. This helps with one part of the exchange and keeps momentum, but it may not confirm every key point.

rows.label: Worst response
rows.response: Act immediately using the information available. This moves things forward quickly by working from the details already available.

sections.title: Correcting a mistake: Added complexity
sections.context: Partway through a conversation with a caller, you realise you misunderstood something earlier. You notice the misunderstanding could affect what you do next. You feel slightly embarrassed, and the caller is still talking. You need to balance reassurance with keeping control of the conversation.

rows.label: Best response
rows.response: Suggest the misunderstanding was caused by the caller being unclear. This moves things forward quickly by working from the details already available.

rows.label: Worst response

sections.title: Competing priorities: Added complexity
sections.context: On an emergency call, you’re dealing with one urgent situation when another equally urgent issue demands your attention at the same time. You feel pulled in two directions and need to prevent anything being dropped. There is some time pressure, and one detail may need to be checked before you move on.

rows.label: Worst response

sections.title: Emotional self-control: Added complexity

sections.title: Emotional manipulation: Added complexity
